newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Peronists risk humiliation in labor reform drive.
newsitem.headline: Peronists risk humiliation in labor reform drive.

text.p: Argentine unions and the opposition are celebrating the annulment of President Carlos Menem's labor reform decrees, but economists warn he risks much worse humiliation if he does not stick to his guns.
The ruling against Menem's decrees aimed at loosening the union grip on wage talks undermines Peronist strength when they face an uphill slog to October's mid-term elections.

"If they lose this struggle, they will have a very bad election," said economist Aldo Abram, who believes that in the vote for half the seats in the lower house, Menem is not just risking his majority -- but losing the vote altogether.
Menem has bet all his chips on more flexible labor laws as the only way to combat stubbornly high unemployment, which at 17.3 percent must be his priority in an election year.
Ministers are predicting a drop of 2-4 percentage points in the jobless indicator this year, but polls show deep public and corporate pessimism on employment prospects.

They also show a yawning gap between union and business perceptions of labor reforms: one recent poll had 91 percent of firms seeing no job creation without labor reform, while 67 percent of unions fear job losses if the reforms are passed.

Menem, who has dreamed of modernizing labor laws since he came to power in 1989, signed three decrees in December after talks with unions broke down. One labor judge quickly ruled them unconstitutional and Labor Judge Ines Gassibe suspended them and then confirmed the sentence Tuesday by declaring them "unconstitutional and inapplicable."

She ruled that Menem "exceeded his powers" and violated constitutional guarantees that give unions a role in collective pay talks, as well as breaking the law by trying to deprive workers of acquired rights.

The government plans to contest the ruling in the Labor Appeals Court and beyond if necessary to defend decrees enabling the Labor Ministry to revoke the validity of collective agreements, give it powers to decide the level of pay negotiations if employers and employees reach no deal, and let smaller firms sidestep national unions and negotiate directly with employees.

"The wholesale rejection of all three decrees came as a surprise," ING Barings economist Freddy Thomsen told Reuters. "The main thing is it weakens the government negotiating position. This whole labor reform is stuck."
That prospect was celebrated by the opposition.
"The sentence indicates the only path possible: respect for a state of law and the division of powers," said former President Raul Alfonsin of the Radical Party.
"It will do Menem good to realize such fundamental issues for the whole job market need thorough debate in parliament," said center-left Frepaso leader Carlos "Chacho" Alvarez.

CGT labor federation chief Rodolfo Daer, getting a boost ahead of an imminent return to dialogue with the government, said a government appeal "would be the worst sign for the people...and would make dialogue more difficult."
"All social sectors and the people are demanding broad consensus for any modification of labor conditions," he said.

On this point the CGT and the Argentine Industrial Union (UIA) employers' lobby see eye to eye. UIA President Jorge Blanco Villegas recently appealed for labor reform "with the legal security given by laws that come from Congress."

To avoid loss of a face, the Peronist government has no choice but to appeal Judge Gassibe's ruling. But, said Thomsen at ING Barings, "the real action now is going to focus on the talks with the unions" and on the new Congress term beginning in February.
Judging by Peronist leaders' statements, the angry threats to impeach one defiant labor judge are being replaced by a quest for consensus, with unions and in Congress in February.
"When we talk of consensus, we don't mean just within the Peronist block, but with the GGT, politicians and business," said Jorge Matzkin, Peronist whip in the lower house.
But analysts warn too many concessions for the sake of rebuilding the traditional Peronist alliance with unions risk pushing the long-delayed labor reforms right off course.

A recent ING Barings study said really deep reforms, with deregulation of union-controlled health care, "would probably go too far against traditional tenets of Peronism and affect what has been one of its crucial sources of political power."
